Manistee|United States of America.f: During the late 1800s lumber boom, Manistee reportedly had more millionaires per capita than anywhere else in the United States.

Bettles|United States of America.f: Bettles is Alaska's second smallest incorporated city, with 23 residents in 2020, and recorded -70 F on January 4, 1975.

Shishmaref|United States of America.f: Shishmaref's shoreline has been eroding at up to 10 feet (3.3 m) per year in recent years.

Red Devil|United States of America.f: The village took its name from the Red Devil Mine, a mercury operation founded in 1921 that ran until 1971.

Tin City|United States of America.f: Tin ore was found on Cape Mountain in July 1902, and a mining camp and post office followed by 1904.

Charlevoix|United States of America.f: Michigan's first nuclear power plant, Big Rock Point, operated at Charlevoix from 1962 to 1997.

Atka|United States of America.f: Atka Island is a shield volcano, and its highest point, Korovin Volcano, last erupted in 2006.

Akutan|United States of America.f: A Japanese Zero flown by Tadayoshi Koga crashed on Akutan Island in June 1942 and was recovered by US forces that July.

Tanana|United States of America.f: Tanana recorded a low of -76 F on January 27, 1989, one of the coldest readings in Alaska.

Togiak Village|United States of America.f: Heavy winter snowfall made gathering firewood hard, so residents moved to the west side of the bay and founded Togiak.

Kotlik|United States of America.f: Kotlik began as a Russian trading post in 1850, and a Russian Orthodox church and cemetery were here before 1867.

Yakataga|United States of America.f: Yakataga's name comes from a Native term meaning canoe road, for two reefs that form a canoe passage to the village.

Roche Harbor|United States of America.f: Roche Harbor's lime company supplied lime for rebuilding San Francisco after the 1906 earthquake.

Beaver Island|United States of America.f: From 1848 to 1856 Beaver Island was a Mormon theocracy and monarchy ruled by King James Strang.

Minchumina|United States of America.f: Lake Minchumina is the nearest settlement to the geographic center of Alaska.

Kobuk|United States of America.f: Kobuk recorded -68 F on March 1, 1971, the coldest March temperature ever measured in the United States.

Nulato|United States of America.f: In 1900 two riverboats a day stopped at Nulato to buy firewood during the Yukon steamboat boom.

Nikolai|United States of America.f: Nikolai was a trading post and roadhouse on the Rainy Pass Trail linking the Ophir gold district to Cook Inlet.

Nelson Lagoon|United States of America.f: A salmon salting station staffed mostly by Scandinavians ran here from 1906 to 1917, so many locals have Scandinavian ancestry.

St Michael|United States of America.f: Founded as a Russian trading post in 1833, St. Michael swelled to as many as 10,000 people during the 1897 gold rush.

Shaktoolik|United States of America.f: Spanish naturalist Felix Rodriguez de la Fuente died in a plane crash at Shaktoolik in 1980 while filming an Iditarod documentary.

Grayling|United States of America.f: Grayling has been an Iditarod checkpoint on odd-numbered years since 1977.

Chalkyitsik|United States of America.f: The Gwich'in name for Chalkyitsik means to fish with a hook, at the mouth of the creek.

Shungnak|United States of America.f: Shungnak comes from the Inupiaq word Isingnaq, meaning jade, a stone found in the surrounding area.

Golovin|United States of America.f: After the 1898 Council gold discovery, Golovin became a supply point, with goods sent across the lagoon and up the Niukluk River.

Point Hope|United States of America.f: Point Hope's ancient Tikigaq site was called the most extensive and complete one-period site in the circumpolar region.

Quinhagak|United States of America.f: The nearby Nunalleq site has yielded over 100,000 artifacts dating from 1350 to 1670.

Alakanuk|United States of America.f: Alakanuk is a Yup'ik word meaning wrong way or mistake village, apt for a spot in a maze of river channels.

Venetie|United States of America.f: The Venetie Indian Reserve, set up in 1941, was the largest reservation in Alaska at about 1.4 million acres.

Allakaket|United States of America.f: In September 1994 floodwaters swept away nearly all of Allakaket's buildings, homes, and winter food caches.

Koyukuk|United States of America.f: Koyukuk was an Iditarod checkpoint in 2015, when the race was rerouted away from Fairbanks.

Noorvik|United States of America.f: Noorvik was the first town counted in the 2010 US census, and its name means a place that is moved to.

Stevens Village|United States of America.f: The village is named for its first chief, Old Steven Stevens, who lived from about 1850 to roughly 1912-1920.

Birch Creek|United States of America.f: Birch Creek grew from a camp that supplied fish to the Hudson's Bay Company at Fort Yukon, first noted in 1862.

Noatak|United States of America.f: Noatak is the only settlement on the Noatak River, which is over 400 miles long, and has no road connection.

Wales|United States of America.f: Wales is the westernmost city on the North American mainland.

Kaltag|United States of America.f: Russians named Kaltag for a Koyukon man called Kaltaga.

Beaver|United States of America.f: Beaver grew after 1907 Chandalar gold strikes as the Yukon River terminus for miners heading north to the gold fields.

Tatitlek|United States of America.f: Tatitlek is the village nearest to the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill, which hit its fishing resources hard.

Eagle|United States of America.f: In 1905 Roald Amundsen used Eagle's telegraph line to Valdez to send news of his Northwest Passage voyage to the world.
